sections.title: Role and Value of Site Characterization
sections.summary: Site characterization informs decision makers about ground conditions so risks (potential losses, usually costs) can be identified and addressed; ground risks are often a project's greatest. Its value: the investigation must cost less than the savings its information produces.
sections.body: Characterization of subsurface conditions is one of the most challenging yet important activities for transportation infrastructure. Its broad purpose is to inform geotechnical specialists, planners, designers, constructors and others about ground conditions so they can identify and address risks; "risk" is a potential for loss, generally financial, quantifiable as a potential cost times its likelihood, including indirect costs from reduced mobility or public safety. Ground risks are commonly the greatest on many projects (Ground Board, 1991) and depend on the quantity and quality of subsurface investigation (Hoek and Palmeiri, 1998; Clayton, 2001). Improved characterization reduces unforeseen conditions (claims, change orders, overruns, poor performance), increases the reliability of soil and rock properties and design parameters (Loehr, et al., 2015), helps identify geotechnical hazards, and reduces construction risk and bid costs. It comes at a cost (p. 1-2); the fundamental value proposition compares the investigation cost with the savings its information permits: will the information let features be designed, built, operated and maintained for less than without it, and will the savings exceed the investigation cost? If so the investigations produce value and are justified. (pp. 1-1 to 1-2)
key_points: Ground risks commonly the greatest on many projects (Ground Board, 1991) (p. 1-1).
Better characterization: fewer claims, more reliable parameters, lower bids (p. 1-1).
Value proposition: savings from the information must exceed investigation cost (p. 1-2).

sections.title: Challenges for Effective Site Characterization
sections.summary: Seven challenges make some uncertainty about ground conditions inevitable: small sampled volume, heterogeneity, complex behavior, many measurement types of unquantified value, early timing, varying groundwater and practical constraints. Characterize to a level set by the value proposition, including the reliability of the information.
sections.body: Challenges include: (1) the volume to characterize is very large compared with the volume sampled or tested; (2) materials are inherently heterogeneous in space and time; (3) soil and rock behavior is complex and hard to replicate in tests; (4) many measurement types exist whose relative value for specific conditions is not quantitatively established; (5) characterization often precedes final structure locations, loads and limit states; (6) behavior depends on groundwater, which varies and is hard to predict (p. 1-3); (7) access, regulatory and budget issues restrict measurements. Some uncertainty is therefore inevitable and perfect characterization impossible; the objective is an acceptable level commensurate with investigation costs and the costs and risks of design, construction and operation, and characterization should include the reliability or uncertainty of the information. The process itself carries risk: appropriate investigations may still miss features, and hindsight may show a scope was insufficient or excessive, but consistent use of the value proposition reduces risk and improves use of funds over an agency's portfolio of projects. (pp. 1-2 to 1-3)
key_points: Seven challenges; some uncertainty is inevitable (pp. 1-2 to 1-3).
Characterize to an acceptable level set by costs and risks (p. 1-3).
Include the reliability or uncertainty of the information (p. 1-3).
Value proposition pays off over an agency's portfolio (p. 1-3).

sections.title: Purpose of Circular
sections.summary: GEC No. 5 aims to improve site characterization practice: a practical reference for planning and executing investigations and interpreting data into reliable design parameters, not prescriptive procedures; it addresses LRFD, risk and reliability, and quantifying variability and uncertainty.
sections.body: The objective of Geotechnical Engineering Circular (GEC) No. 5 is to improve site characterization practice among agencies, consultants and contractors for transportation features. It is a comprehensive, practical reference for planning and executing investigations and interpreting data into reliable design parameters; it is not intended to provide prescriptive procedures or dictate test methods (p. 1-4) but to guide identification and characterization of hazards, interpretation of properties from field and laboratory measurements and, most importantly, establishing reliable design parameter values from collective interpretation of measurements. It addresses load and resistance factor design (LRFD) and explicit awareness of risk and reliability, provides methods to quantify variability and uncertainty in design parameters, and methods to assess the value of characterization practices for technical and non-technical decision makers. Intended users include geotechnical engineers, engineering geologists, geologists, civil, structural and construction engineers and construction managers. (pp. 1-3 to 1-4)
key_points: Practical reference, not prescriptive procedures (pp. 1-3 to 1-4).
Reliable design parameters from collective interpretation of measurements (p. 1-4).
Addresses LRFD and quantifies variability and uncertainty (p. 1-4).
sections.applicability: Scope and organization of FHWA GEC-5 Geotechnical Site Characterization manual

sections.title: Organization of Circular
sections.summary: Chapters: 2 objectives and products; 3 planning and scoping; 4 classification; 5 problematic soil and rock; 6-10 properties from tests (consolidation, strength, stiffness, rock, hydraulic); 11 design parameters from collections of measurements; 12 hazards; 13 reporting. A property is a measurable characteristic; a parameter is an input to a model or method.
sections.body: The manual emphasizes interpretation of design parameters and, to a lesser extent, hazards. Chapter 2 covers objectives, products and uses of investigations; Chapter 3 planning and scoping, including the relative value of measurement types, remote sensing and geophysics, and scope development; Chapter 4 classification from index properties; Chapter 5 problematic soil and rock types (p. 1-5). Chapters 6 to 10 interpret properties from individual tests: consolidation (6), soil strength (7), stress-strain and stiffness (8), rock (9), hydraulic properties and groundwater (10). The manual uses "property" for a specific characteristic of soil or rock, generally directly measurable (mineralogy, water content, Atterberg limits, unit weight, strength, compressibility), and "parameter" for a term or variable in a model or design method; a "design parameter" is a required input to a design method and may represent an interpretation of properties over an area or volume (e.g., Mohr-Coulomb parameters), so some properties serve as design parameters but not all design parameters are properties. Chapter 11 interprets design parameters from collections of measurements, judgment and the observational method (p. 1-6), stratigraphy, direct and indirect measurements, historical data, and explicit calculation of variability and uncertainty. Chapter 12 covers hazards (karst, mines, seismic, groundwater, landslides, landfills); Chapter 13 documentation and reporting. Appendix 1 summarizes AASHTO and ASTM standards; Appendix 2 gives three site characterization examples; Appendix 3 documents methods for quantifying variability and uncertainty. (pp. 1-4 to 1-6)
key_points: Chapters 6 to 10: properties from individual tests (p. 1-5).
Property = measurable characteristic; parameter = model or design input (p. 1-5).
Chapter 11: design parameters and their variability and uncertainty (pp. 1-5 to 1-6).
Appendices: standards, three examples, variability methods (p. 1-6).
